Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

vignette: Ethan had always been a straight-line kind of man. At twenty-nine, a European-American with a neat moustache, he stood on the edge of the Atlantic as a Coast Guard officer, his uniform crisp, his watch ticking. He married a graphic designer two years ago, and the small apartment they shared on the waterfront was a quiet haven-until the night he was mugged. The memory of that night lived in disjointed fragments, refusing to coalesce into a single story, and that is what has kept him from the peace he and his wife have been yearning for. On a damp evening in early March, after a long shift on the rescue boat, Ethan walked down the cracked concrete of the harbor's parking lot. The sky had turned a bruised purple, and the streetlights flickered like nervous fireflies. As he crossed the intersection, a figure stepped out from a shadowed corner-tall, hooded, eyes narrowed. The stranger pressed a flashlight beam into Ethan's face and demanded his wallet. Ethan's hand trembled, but he did not shout. He slid the wallet into the stranger's palm and watched him retreat into the night, leaving a thin smear of darkness on his shoulder. That night he could not articulate the experience. In the quiet of his apartment, he sat on the edge of the bed, the hum of the air conditioner filling the silence. He tried to describe the scene to his wife, but the words eluded him. "I can't put it into words," he said, the frustration in his voice echoing the emptiness he felt. When he recalled the event, he was numb, as if the memory belonged to someone else. He could see the outlines-the flicker of the flashlight, the roughness of the thief's palm-but the emotional color was missing, a blankness that made the recollection feel distant and detached. Even when he pressed his fingertips to his chest, hoping to summon the adrenaline he remembered feeling in his chest, the surge of fear was absent, replaced by a flat, almost mechanical awareness. The memory did not come in one continuous stream. Instead, it came in disjointed pieces. He could recall the rustle of the stranger's jacket, the way his own breath felt shallow for a breath before the hand had closed over his wallet. He could recall the feeling of the cold metal of the flash drive that the robber had left behind-a small, inconsequential detail that seemed to hold more weight than the full event. Yet the larger narrative remained a puzzle with missing pieces. He could not connect the sound of the streetlights flickering to the sudden chill that ran down his spine. The fragmented nature of the memory made him question his own reliability, worrying that he was missing something essential, that the story he didn't have was dangerous. The way the memory behaved in his mind influenced his daily life in ways that were hard to explain. When Ethan drove back to the base, the roar of the diesel engines and the smell of fresh fuel would occasionally trigger a momentary flash of that dim parking lot. He would sit in his car, eyes narrowed, trying to anchor himself in the present, but the image would surface in a half-formed shape, a jarring silhouette of a stranger's silhouette and the glint of a flashlight. He would find himself looking around as if searching for a threat that was never there, his mind replaying the fragments in quick, disjointed flashes. He was sure that each fragment was a warning, a reminder that danger was always a step behind him, yet the overall picture was incomplete, a broken mirror reflecting a threat that he could not fully grasp. Ethan's work demanded constant vigilance. As a Coast Guard officer, he was expected to be alert to threats on the water. His ability to focus on the horizon, to spot a vessel in distress, was tested every day. Yet the memory that lingered in his mind made it difficult for him to fully immerse himself in the present. When his supervisor asked him to give a briefing, Ethan felt a strange pressure building up inside his chest. He could not put the event into words, but the disjointed fragments were there, a silent echo that made him feel detached from the responsibility he was supposed to hold. He worried that the dissonance between what he remembered and what he needed to do could compromise his performance and, more importantly, the safety of his crew. When he tried to talk to his wife about it, she would watch him with concern, offering a warm hand on his arm, but she could not fully understand the way the memory fractured his thoughts. He feared that he was losing control over his own story, that he was no longer a coherent whole. What he feared most was that the disjointed memory would lead him to misinterpret future events, to mistake ordinary interactions for danger. He was hoping, at the same time, to find a way to piece together those fragments, to give his mind a complete narrative that would allow him to feel whole again. The day he finally decided to seek help was the day he could no longer bear the silent, fragmented echo that kept replaying in the corners of his mind.
